problem: Prior LLM planners for robots mostly work in fully observed or pre-explored scenes, usually table-top or single-room, and handle navigation or manipulation separately. When the full scene graph is dumped to the LLM as a raw object list or JSON, as in SayPlan, it fails in large unexplored, interactive apartments. Existing object-search methods (ESC, VLFM, PONI) score frontiers pairwise and cannot handle targets hidden behind closed doors or inside drawers and cabinets.
motivation: Household mobile manipulation needs long-horizon reasoning over many rooms and objects in unknown, changing environments, where doors must be opened and receptacles searched. LLMs carry useful commonsense priors about where objects are found, but they hallucinate on long, unstructured contexts. The authors argue that a compact, structured, dynamically updated scene-graph encoding, tied to an object-centric action space, lets LLMs make efficient exploration and exploitation decisions. They also argue that success rate and SPL under one fixed time budget hide efficiency differences between methods.
key_idea: Build an open-vocabulary hierarchical 3D scene graph online (dense map → Voronoi graph → door-based room segmentation → LLM room classification), turn it into a compact structured text prompt that includes semantically labelled frontiers, binned distances, object states and a position-realigned action history, and let a frozen GPT-4 choose object-centric high-level actions (navigate / go_to_and_open / close / explore / done) that low-level subpolicies execute.
insight: The structure of the language encoding matters more than just giving the LLM the scene graph. Feeding the same graph as SayPlan-style JSON drops results from SR 97.7 / SPL 63.6 / AUC-E 87.2 to 86.3 / 59.4 / 77.6, with about twice as many infeasible actions (0.41 vs 0.19). The ablations show that explicitly encoding frontiers ('unexplored area' within rooms vs. leading out) is the most important component: without it, SR falls to 79.4 and AUC-E to 72.2. Removing the action history costs less (94.9 / 84.1), and a coarse visited-rooms history recovers most of the gap (97.1 / 86.6). Dropping distance adjectives causes a small SPL drop (61.5). Door-based room segmentation beats Hydra's constriction-based segmentation both in segmentation quality (precision 0.666 vs 0.621, purity 0.615 vs 0.562) and in downstream SR (97.7 vs 92.0). The policy tolerates heavy under-segmentation even though closed-set room-category accuracy is only 27.6% in iGibson.
method: Dynamic RGB-D mapping: posed RGB-D frames with semantics are fused into a 3D voxel grid, and highest occupied stixels give a BEV occupancy map plus a free-space map (floor/carpet), updated as objects and doors change.

Navigational Voronoi graph: the BEV map is inflated via ESDF, a Generalized Voronoi Diagram is computed, points near obstacles are pruned, the largest connected component is kept, and the graph is sparsified (Hydra-like).

Door-based room segmentation and scene graph: a Gaussian KDE over observed door centers (bandwidth 2.0) cuts Voronoi edges in high-density regions into room components. Room adjacency comes from shortest paths crossing exactly two rooms. Objects are assigned to rooms by minimizing path(n_o, n_vp) + d(o, n_o)^1.3 + d(vp, n_vp) from the viewpoint where they were seen, which avoids assignments through walls.
Open-set room classification: GPT-3.5-turbo labels each room cluster freely from its contained object categories, recomputed at every high-level step.

Object-centric high-level action space: navigate(room, object) via A* on the explored BEV map (success within 1.5 m), go_to_and_open, close, explore(room) to a room's frontier (within 0.5 m), and done(). The closest instance resolves ambiguities.

Structured grounded prompt: lists rooms with their objects, including counts and open/closed states. A* distances are binned into adjectives (very close ≤3, near ≤10, far ≤20, distant). Frontiers are split via hole-filling into in-room 'unexplored area' vs frontiers leading out. The prompt also carries the last h actions, realigned to the current rooms via Voronoi-node matching of interaction positions, plus success/failure/invalid-argument feedback.

Re-planning: infeasible or unparsable commands continue the conversation ('The last action ... failed'), and the episode ends after more than 5 such failures. Executed but failed subpolicies trigger a fresh re-encoding of the scene with updated history. A new evaluation metric, AUC-E, is the area under the success-vs-budget efficiency curve up to 5000 low-level steps, with each object interaction weighted as 30 steps.

setting.backbone: gpt-4-1106-preview (frozen) for high-level reasoning; gpt-3.5-turbo-1106 (frozen) for room classification; classical A*/Voronoi subpolicies in sim, ROS NavStack + pretrained N2M2 manipulation policies on the real robot
setting.training_data: none (training-free); prompts and hyperparameters (e.g., KDE bandwidth) tuned on the 8 iGibson training scenes
setting.observation: posed RGB-D (256x256, 120° vFOV, 5 m range) with ground-truth semantic/instance segmentation, GT localization, articulated-object state and handle detection
setting.action_space: high-level object-centric actions (navigate, go_to_and_open, close, explore(room), done) executed by subpolicies over low-level actions: forward 7.5 cm, turn left/right, open/close articulated object ('magic' actions in sim), done
setting.simulator: iGibson (15 interactive apartments, Fetch robot scaled 0.85) + real-world apartment with Toyota HSR
setting.privileged: GT semantic segmentation/instances, GT depth and localization, GT open/closed state of articulated objects, handle detection, magic open/close actions in sim; real world uses a pre-recorded LiDAR map annotated with semantic labels (revealed as observed) for semantics and localization, plus AR markers for handles

numbers_note: Efficiency curves are given only as a figure (Fig. 5). Scene-segmentation results (precision 0.666 / recall 0.948 / purity 0.615 vs Hydra 0.621 / 0.943 / 0.562) and room-category accuracy (27.6% iGibson closed-set, 90.1% real-world open-set) are reported separately. Fuzzy-search tasks are qualitative only (human-judged). Own ablations not listed above: w/ room-history SR 97.1 / SPL 63.0 / AUC-E 86.6; w/o distances SR 97.1 / SPL 61.5 / AUC-E 86.4.
results: On a new semantic interactive object search task in 7 unseen iGibson apartments (175 episodes), MoMa-LLM reaches SR 97.7 / SPL 63.6 / AUC-E 87.2. It beats the strongest baseline, ESC-Interactive (95.4 / 62.7 / 84.5), and clearly beats HIMOS RL (93.7 / 48.5 / 77.4) and a SayPlan-style Unstructured LLM (86.3 / 59.4 / 77.6), while opening fewer objects and travelling less. On a real Toyota HSR in a 4-room apartment it ties ESC at 80% success but nearly halves distance travelled (17.9 vs 33.9 m) and object interactions (2.2 vs 3.5). It also handles fuzzy queries such as 'find me something for breakfast'.
limitations: Assumes ground-truth perception (semantic segmentation, depth, localization, handle detection, object state); sim manipulation uses 'magic' open/close actions, and the real world relies on a pre-annotated semantic map and AR markers.
Door-based room segmentation under-segments open layouts (e.g., combined kitchen/living room); closed-set room-category accuracy in iGibson is only 27.6%.

LLM API latency dominates reasoning time (~7.5 s per step in sim; high-level reasoning is 45% of real-world runtime). The scene graph is fully recomputed each step. Evaluation uses only 7 test scenes and 10 real-world episodes.
